extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology and creative writers studying narrative temporality
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, classify, and analyze anachronies (analepses/prolepses), their scope and effects within a narrative, and how they structure beginnings, embeddings, and macro/micro temporal architecture. Useful for narratological analysis or for designing complex temporal strategies in creative writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish narrative sections from chronological positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize separate narrative 'sections' (A, B, C...) and map them to story-time 'positions' (1,2,3...), noting that sections can occupy the same temporal position while differing in hierarchical level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use labelled formulae (e.g., A4-B3-C5...) to track which narrative sections correspond to which chronological moments; observe hierarchical interlocking (e.g., M depends on L which depends on K...). Example: Proust fragment mapped fifteen narrative sections to nine temporal positions to reveal interdependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify anachronies as analepses or prolepses; prefer 'anachrony' as neutral term
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify retrojections (analepses/flashbacks) and anticipations (prolepses/flashforwards). Note terminological issues with Greek roots and the usefulness of the neutral term 'anachrony'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of etymological complications (lepse- vs lapsis-root confusion) and when to adopt alternative terms (e.g., allachrony) to avoid misleading oppositions; treat prolepsis/analepsis as members of a grammatical-rhetorical family useful for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate prolepsis from ellipsis (acceleration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish true prolepses (anticipations that presuppose a return or narrative relation) from mere ellipses, which are leaps forward in narrative time without a return and function as accelerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the transition to a later position never returns to the earlier one, mark it as an ellipsis/acceleration (use a hyphen in formulaic notation) rather than a prolepsis bracket; e.g., transition from C5 to D6 in the Proust fragment is an ellipsis: C5 - D6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure anachrony's reach and extent
rubrics_metrics.description: For any anachrony, assess (1) reach — the temporal distance between the first-narrative present and the anachrony's temporal field; and (2) extent — the duration of story-time the anachrony covers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples: Ulysses' wound analepsis has a reach of several decades and an extent of a few days. Reach and extent are measurable and help categorize the anachrony's narrative function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether analepsis is external, internal, or mixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify analepses as external (their entire extent lies outside the first narrative's temporal field), internal (their temporal field is contained within the first narrative), or mixed (reach/back-and-forth spanning before and after the first narrative's beginning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External analepses typically 'fill out' antecedents without interfering with the first narrative (e.g., Un amour de Swann); internal analepses risk redundancy or collision and require more careful handling in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate homodiegetic vs heterodiegetic internal analepses
rubrics_metrics.description: Within internal analepses, distinguish heterodiegetic ones (deal with a different diegetic line from the first narrative) from homodiegetic ones (deal with the same line of action as the first narrative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heterodiegetic internal analepses (e.g., a character's antecedents) usually do not interfere with the first narrative's prerogatives. Homodiegetic internal analepses directly risk redundancy and narrative collision and must be analyzed as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify completing analepses ('returns')
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize completing analepses — retrospective sections that fill earlier gaps in the narrative (temporal ellipses) and repair omissions after the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completing analepses are used to fill ellipses (e.g., Marcel's 1914 Paris stay recounted during a 1916 visit) and can also repair lateral omissions like paralipsis when details omitted earlier are later supplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify repeating analepses ('recalls')
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize repeating analepses — narrative recalls where the text retraces its own path, often compact and allusive, creating deliberate reiteration rather than filling a gap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These recalls are typically short but crucial for narrative economy (e.g., Proust's involuntary-memory reminiscences at the Guermantes matinee). They may emphasize analogy or contrast between past and present scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize paralipsis (lateral omission) and its retrospective filling
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify paralipsis as omission not of a temporal segment but of a constituent element (e.g., a character or situation) within periods the narrative does cover; such omissions can be later supplied by analepses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Swann's death effects omitted in place and later reported; Marcel's omission of a 'girl-cousin' episode from the Combray narrative is lateral omission later revealed. Treat paralipsis as different from temporal ellipsis and consider its thematic implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect iterative analepses/iterative ellipses
rubrics_metrics.description: When retrospection refers generically to a class ('a winter') or to repeated series (multiple similar episodes), identify the analepsis or ellipsis as iterative rather than pinpointing a unique event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterative retrospections are often expressed in imperfect/repetitive aspect and may synthesize entire series of events (e.g., a single dinner standing in for many prior dinners) to achieve tonal or thematic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze risk of interference for internal analepses
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal analepses that fall within the first narrative's temporal field can cause redundancy or collision with the first narrative; these interference risks must be examined and categorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish cases where interference is harmless (heterodiegetic) from those where completion vs recall strategies are used to manage overlap; consider narrative devices (paralipsis, ellipsis, recall) that mitigate or exploit interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formulaic/bracketing notation to represent temporal structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent complex temporal architectures with notational formulas and brackets (e.g., A4[B3]C5...), where bracket openings indicate dynamic relationships (analepses/prolepses) and closings correspond to returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notation makes hierarchical interlockings explicit and helps visualize which sections open anachronies and how subordination operates across levels; note that dynamic relationships tend to come at openings of brackets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish micronarrative (microstructure) from macrostructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate analyses at micro (section-level, fine-grained temporal positions) and macro (book-level, large articulations) scales; micro details are simplified when moving to macrostructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When shifting scale, proceed by 'very crude simplification' and avoid conflating details belonging to other scales; macro analysis focuses on principal articulations (e.g., central transfer point controlling movement across the whole work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify central transfer points or control positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect narrative centers or 'transfer points' (e.g., Proust's position 5 — the insomnias/madeleine) that function as indispensable hubs from which analepses are launched and to which returns are made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These positions act as dispatching narratives that control movement across the work (5-2-5-5'...) and may remain central even when excentric in diegetic chronology; mapping them reveals narrative propulsion and organizing strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize multiple beginnings/exordia as a narrative strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify when a text multiplies 'beginnings' (absolute, ostensible, resumption, real, etc.) especially through memory-created instances, producing several exordia that collectively launch the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proust's Recherche exemplifies multiple beginnings (first beginning: insomnia sentence; later beginnings: Combray chapters, madeleine episode, ab ovo Swann novella, etc.). Each beginning may function as a prologue or as the real initiation of the autobiographical movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for involuntary-memory recalls as a distinctive analeptic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat involuntary-memory reminiscences (e.g., the madeleine, Venice, the row of trees) as a specific kind of recall that is euphoric, associative, and often foregrounds comparison between present and past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These memory-driven recalls can be formally similar to repeating analepses but carry affective and epistemic functions (revealing previously buried material, creating analogies/contrasts) and are central to narrative dynamics in works like Proust's.
